content.text: The one inspection-type right in the document (p0114, source code escrow) runs **in our favour** against Garman, confirming there is no audit right binding us. Resubmitting the finding with that point made explicit.

input.quote: Sparkling may itself or by retaining independent experts, examine and test the materials for compliance with the obligations of Garman hereunder
input.rationale: No audit, inspection, licence-verification or system-access right runs against Sparkling anywhere in the Agreement. Regex and literal searches for audit / inspect / verif / examin / records / premises / access / remote, plus full reads of § 3 (Restrictions on Use), § 14 (Confidentiality) and § 20 (General Matters), return no such right: § 3 imposes substantive use restrictions only, with no verification, reporting or self-certification mechanic; § 14 is a mutual confidentiality provision whose reference to "accounting records for which access is obtained" is a definitional carve-in, not a grant of access; and the only "access" in § 10 is Garman's telephone support provided to us. The single examination right in the document (§ 16 escrow, p0114) runs in our favour, permitting Sparkling and its independent experts to examine and test the escrow materials for Garman's compliance. Because there is no audit right binding us, there is nothing to constrain on frequency, notice, business hours, auditor independence, cost allocation or system access, and the outcome is better than the playbook preferred position. The failed deterministic check ("audit frequency limited") is a direct consequence of the total absence of an audit clause rather than a defect in the drafting: the AUDIT rule exists to cap a Vendor-favourable right, so its absence benefits our party and is correctly treated as compliant rather than missing. No redline or comment is proposed, since raising the point would invite Garman to introduce a verification right we do not currently owe.
